    Seestar setup

    Add the star as a custom object using these J2000 coordinates.
    ----
    Turn on "save each frame" before you start. On 12 September we lost the first 24 frames because it was off. Without the individual frames there is no light curve.

    Conditions

    Finder chart

    North up, east left, 5.2° across. The dashed box is one Seestar S30 Pro frame (3.9° × 2.2°); its tilt on the sky changes through the night.

    Comparison star suggestions

    Differential photometry needs stars of similar brightness and colour in the same frame. These are the best matches from the Hipparcos catalogue within 1.1° of the target, so they stay in frame however it rotates.

    Hipparcos is complete only to about magnitude 9, so fainter good comparison stars exist that are not listed. HOPS can also pick them automatically. Avoid any star marked as variable.

    Transit predictor

    This works the same way as the Swarthmore Tapir tool we used for the booklet, so the list keeps going instead of ending in May 2027. With the default settings it reproduces all 126 booklet events, with mid-times matching to within about half a minute.

    Settings

    The booklet lists a 33° minimum, but every event in it, and every suggested window, actually follows 35°. The predictor uses 35° by default so it matches the booklet.

    Add your own planet

    Any transiting planet can be predicted from Campbell River. Take the numbers from the NASA Exoplanet Archive or ExoClock. Your planets are saved in this browser only.

        The #1 Star Candidate

        HD 189733, also catalogued as V452 Vulpeculae, is the top-ranked star in our catalog. It sits 15.5′ east of the Dumbbell Nebula, close enough that both fit in one Seestar frame.

        This photo was stacked from frames taken during our HD 189733 b transit session on the night of 12–13 September 2026. We plate-solved it for this page: we found the stars in the image, matched them against the Hipparcos catalog, and fitted the mapping between pixels and sky coordinates. That fit tells us exactly which dot is our star.

        Magnified 3× around HD 189733. The gold ring is the plate-solved catalog position, carried forward to the date of the photo.

        Targets

        The 12 host stars in the catalog, in rank order. Open any star for its profile and a simulated light curve showing roughly what its transit should look like on our instrument.

        HD 189733 b margin 21.2× rank 1

        HD 189733 is one of the brightest stars known to host a transiting hot Jupiter, and it doubles as its own variable star, cataloged as V452 Vulpeculae because starspots slowly modulate its brightness as the star rotates. Its planet, HD 189733 b, was discovered in 2005 and completes an orbit in just over two days, producing a deep, easily measured 2.4 percent dip in brightness. Because the star is so bright and the transit so deep, this system has become a standard first target for both professional atmospheric studies and amateur transit photometry.

        WASP-33 b margin 9.0× rank 8

        WASP-33, also cataloged as HD 15082, is an A-type star spinning so quickly that its own light varies in brightness independent of its planet, making it the first star ever confirmed to be both a delta Scuti pulsating variable and an exoplanet host. Its planet, WASP-33 b, orbits in just 1.22 days on a retrograde, tilted path relative to the star's own spin. Because the star's pulsations ripple through the light curve, this target is scientifically interesting but genuinely more complex to analyze than most, since part of what shows up in the data is starlight variability, not just the planet.

        HD 209458 b margin 13.2× rank 6

        HD 209458 holds a permanent place in the history of exoplanet science. In 1999 it became the first star ever observed to have a planet transit in front of it, and its planet, nicknamed Osiris, went on to become the first exoplanet confirmed to have an atmosphere at all. The planet is only slightly less massive than Jupiter but noticeably larger, giving it a low density consistent with a puffed up, highly irradiated gas giant. Its brightness, magnitude 7.7, and its 1.5 percent transit depth make it a very approachable target for a modest amateur telescope.

        KELT-20 b margin 14.5× rank 4

        KELT-20 is a hot, fast spinning A-type star that hosts one of the most extreme planets in this catalog. KELT-20 b is classified as an ultra-hot Jupiter, meaning its dayside temperature is pushed to roughly 2300 Kelvin by the intense radiation of its host star. The star itself is quite young, only about 58 million years old, and is among the brightest known hosts of a transiting giant planet. Astronomers have already detected sodium, iron, and other metals directly in the planet's atmosphere using this same transit method.

        KELT-4 A b margin 3.6× rank 97

        KELT-4 A is the brightest known host star of a hot Jupiter that sits inside a hierarchical triple star system, meaning it has two additional stellar companions, KELT-4 B and C, orbiting the system as a close pair further out. The planet, KELT-4 A b, is a typical hot Jupiter on a three day orbit, discovered in 2016. Because two extra stars share the field of view, careful comparison star selection matters even more than usual when measuring this system's transit.

        HAT-P-22 b margin 4.8× rank 49

        HAT-P-22 is a G-type dwarf star very close in character to the Sun, located in the constellation Ursa Major, with a faint red dwarf companion orbiting far out in the same system. Its planet, HAT-P-22 b, is a genuinely massive hot Jupiter, over twice the mass of Jupiter itself, discovered in 2010. The host star has the lowest mass of any star in its original discovery survey's comparison sample, making this a useful benchmark system for studying how a lower mass star supports a heavy planet in a tight orbit.

        KELT-17 b margin 4.0× rank 90

        KELT-17 is an unusual host star known as an Am star, short for metallic-line A star, a class of chemically peculiar star whose atmosphere shows an overabundance of certain heavy elements like titanium, chromium, and iron. It was the first exoplanet host ever confirmed to belong to this specific chemical class. Its planet, KELT-17 b, orbits in just over three days and was discovered in 2016 using Doppler tomography, a technique that measures how tilted a planet's orbit is relative to its star's spin.

        TOI-1518 b margin 4.8× rank 68

        TOI-1518 is a hot F0-type star discovered by NASA's TESS mission to host one of the more extreme ultra-hot Jupiters in this catalog. TOI-1518 b orbits in under two days and is inflated to nearly twice the radius of Jupiter, with iron directly detected in its atmosphere, a rare and notable find that makes it a strong candidate for future spectroscopy aimed at detecting a thermal inversion layer. At magnitude 9.0, it sits at the fainter end of what this project's search criteria allow, but its very deep transit helps compensate.

        KELT-7 b margin 5.4× rank 38

        KELT-7 orbits the brightest star of any planet discovered by the entire KELT survey, an F-type star spinning rapidly enough to make precise radial velocity measurements difficult. KELT-7 b is a substantial hot Jupiter, roughly 1.4 times the mass of Jupiter, discovered in 2015, and has since been studied with the James Webb Space Telescope, which found evidence of a metal-enriched atmosphere. Its brightness and depth make it one of the more forgiving targets in this catalog.

        K2-232 b margin 3.3× rank 125

        K2-232 is a late F-type star observed by NASA's K2 mission, and its planet, K2-232 b, stands out for its unusually elongated, eccentric orbit rather than the nearly circular path most hot Jupiters follow. Classified as a warm Saturn, the planet takes over eleven days to complete one orbit, considerably longer than most targets in this catalog, and is one of only a handful of well characterized warm giant planets with a host star brighter than tenth magnitude. Its long period means suitable transit windows appear far less often than for the tighter orbiting hot Jupiters elsewhere in this list.

        HAT-P-1 b margin 4.8× rank 51

        HAT-P-1 is one half of a wide visual binary system, paired with an almost identical Sun-like star roughly 1500 astronomical units away, a companion close enough in brightness and color that astronomers have used it as a built in comparison star for unusually precise differential photometry. Its planet, HAT-P-1 b, was discovered in 2006 and is notably large and low density for its mass, a puzzle that helped motivate later theoretical models of how irradiation inflates close-in giant planets. The wide binary companion is a genuine practical advantage for amateur observers too, since a bright, reliable comparison star sits right in the same field.

        Method

        How the catalog was searched and how each event is ranked.

        ParameterValue used
        Observing coordinatesLatitude 50.0163° N, Longitude 125.2461° W
        TimezonePacific Time (PST8PDT)
        Minimum elevation, ingress and egress33°, combined with AND logic
        Minimum V magnitudebrighter than V = 12.0
        Minimum transit depth6 ppt (0.6%)
        Out-of-transit baseline1.5 hours before ingress and after egress
        Night definitionNautical twilight (Sun at −12° altitude)
        Search window250 days from date of search

        Ranking method

        Each event is ranked by an estimated detection margin: how many multiples of the expected photometric noise floor the transit depth represents on a 30mm optical system. A 10 second, in-focus exposure of a V=7.7 star was measured to collect roughly 26,000 electrons on the sensor. Scaling that to any other magnitude, and binning across a fixed 5 minute window, gives an expected precision at that magnitude. The margin is simply the transit depth divided by that expected precision.

        M(V, d) = d × 883.2 × 10−0.2(V − 7.7)

        V is the host star's apparent magnitude, d is the transit depth as a decimal fraction, M is the resulting margin. Ties are broken first by percent of transit plus baseline observable, then by moon illumination.

        Simulated light curves

        Every chart on this page, in each star's profile and in the printed reference this site mirrors, shares one fixed grid: the same horizontal and vertical scale across every target, so a shorter, shallower transit appears visibly narrower and shallower than a longer, deeper one when compared side by side. Ingress and egress are modeled as a smooth transition rather than a hard-edged shape, consistent with the gradual way a planet's disk covers and uncovers its star, though the model does not include stellar limb darkening. Simulated data points carry random noise scaled to each target's own detection margin, so a low-margin target's chart shows visibly more scatter than a high-margin one, and each star's plotted points span only that star's own baseline-and-transit window, not the full grid.

        Detection margin calculator

        Check any star, including ones outside this catalog, against the same formula. Margin above about 5 is comfortable; below 3 the dip is hard to separate from noise.

        After the night

        Turning a folder of frames into a light curve. These are the steps in HOPS (HOlomon Photometric Software), the tool the team uses.

        1. Copy every frame off the SeestarKeep the original FITS files from the session folder, not just the stacked image. Each frame becomes one point on the light curve.
        2. Select data and targetPoint HOPS at the folder, pick the target (HOPS can look it up by name) and confirm the exposure time and observing site.
        3. Run reductionHOPS calibrates and prepares every frame. Expect this to take a while on several hundred frames.
        4. Inspect framesReject frames with clouds, trailing, satellites or bad focus. Rejected frames simply leave gaps.
        5. Run alignmentHOPS matches stars between frames so the same star is measured each time even as the field drifts and rotates.
        6. PhotometryChoose the target and several comparison stars of similar brightness and colour. Avoid known variables.
        7. Exoplanet fittingFit the transit model. Compare the fitted depth, duration and mid-time against this catalog's predictions.

        Share the result

        A detected transit, or a well-documented non-detection, is useful to professional ephemeris programs.

        ExoClock, the ESA Ariel ephemeris project Exoplanet Transit Database (ETD), Czech Astronomical Society AAVSO Exoplanet Section HOPS software (ExoWorlds Spies)
        Variable star practice first: reproducing a published variable star light curve with the same pipeline proves the process before trusting a transit result.

        Check a light curve

        Drop in a light curve exported from HOPS (or any text or CSV file with time and relative flux columns). The site finds the predicted transit in your data, fits the dip and compares it with the prediction. Nothing is uploaded; it all runs in your browser.

        Reference

        Limitations, terms and sources.

        Limitations

        The margin-based ranking on this page measures one thing: how strong a transit's signal should be relative to instrument noise. It does not account for weather, and that's worth being direct about.

        Historical climate averages for Campbell River show the sky clear or better, meaning partly cloudy or less, for close to half of an average day in September, the start of this catalog's search window, and closer to a fifth of an average day by January, the middle of it. September averages about 47% clear-or-better sky, October about 36%, and January, the cloudiest month on record, only about 22.5%. These figures describe an average day, not specifically the night, so they're a seasonal trend, not a forecast for any single date.

        Combining that with an event's own percent of transit plus baseline observable gives a rougher, more honest picture of real odds. HD 189733 b's September 12 event, rank 1 in this catalog, is 92% geometrically observable in a month averaging roughly 47% clear-or-better sky:

        0.92 × 0.47 ≈ 0.43

        Even the single best ranked night in the entire catalog carries a real world success probability closer to two in five than to certain, once weather is factored in. This is a seasonal average, not a forecast, and doesn't account for cloud clustering, equipment reliability, or human error, none of which have a solid regional figure behind them. A strong rank is necessary but not sufficient for a successful night.

        Source: historical climate averages for Campbell River, BC, compiled from long-term station data (approximately 1990-2020).

        Every event was generated with the Swarthmore College Transit/Eclipse Observability tool (Tapir; Jensen 2013), cross-referenced against the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Discovery papers for all 12 systems are cited in the printed reference booklet.

        Sky map: star positions, magnitudes and colours, constellation lines, the Milky Way outline and the Messier catalog come from d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD licence), derived from the HYG database (David Nash) and the Hipparcos catalog. Moon and Sun positions use the low-precision methods in Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms (1998). Precession uses the IAU 1976 model (Lieske et al. 1977).

        KELT-19 A coordinates: Exoplanet Transit Database, Czech Astronomical Society, consistent with Siverd et al. (2018). These were added to this site in November 2026 and are not in the printed booklet.

        Cloud forecasts: Open-Meteo.com, licensed CC BY 4.0. The live predictor uses the same linear ephemerides as the booklet; for planets with only two booklet events, published periods (consistent with the booklet to within 1.4 s per orbit) are used.

        Tapir, Swarthmore College   NASA Exoplanet Archive

        Predicted times carry uncertainty from each system's published ephemeris, and it grows with the number of orbits since the reference epoch. Re-check a date shortly before relying on it.

        Glossary

        Observational and timing terms

        Transit
        The event this whole page is built around: a planet passing directly between its host star and an observer, blocking a small, measurable fraction of the star's light.
        Occultation
        A related but distinct event in which one body is completely hidden behind another. A transit is a partial blocking by a smaller foreground body; an occultation is a full disappearance behind a larger one.
        Light curve
        A graph of a star's brightness over time. The core data product of this entire project: a transit shows up as a temporary dip in an otherwise flat light curve.
        Photometry
        The general technique of measuring an object's brightness. Differential photometry is one specific approach to it.
        Ingress
        The beginning of a transit, when the planet first begins to cross in front of the star.
        Egress
        The end of a transit, when the planet finishes crossing the star's disk.
        Mid-transit
        The moment the planet is at the center of its crossing, when brightness is lowest.
        Transit depth
        The fraction of starlight blocked at mid-transit, in parts per thousand (ppt) or percent.
        Parts per thousand (ppt)
        A unit for very small fractions. A depth of 10 ppt means the star dims by 1.0% at mid-transit.
        Baseline
        Observation time before ingress and after egress, used to establish the star's normal brightness.
        BJD_TDB − 2,450,000
        Barycentric Julian Date with 2,450,000 subtracted to keep figures short. Add it back for the full date.
        Julian Date
        A continuous count of days used in astronomy instead of the calendar, avoiding the ambiguity of months and years when timing events precisely.
        Right ascension
        A star's east-west position on the sky, astronomy's equivalent of longitude, measured in hours, minutes, and seconds.
        Declination
        A star's north-south position on the sky, astronomy's equivalent of latitude, measured in degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds.
        Elevation / Airmass
        Elevation is the star's angle above the horizon. Airmass (1/sin of elevation) measures how much atmosphere its light passes through; higher airmass means more distortion and noise.
        Nautical twilight
        The point at which the Sun is 12° below the horizon, used as this project's definition of usable darkness.
        Differential photometry
        A measurement technique comparing a target star's brightness against nearby comparison stars in the same image, canceling out atmospheric and instrumental variation.
        Ephemeris
        A table or formula predicting the position or timing of an astronomical event, based on a known orbital period and reference epoch.
        Detection margin
        How many multiples of the expected photometric noise floor a transit's depth represents on this project's instrument. See the Method section above for the formula.
        Aperture
        The diameter of a telescope's main light-collecting lens or mirror. A larger aperture gathers more light, directly improving how faint or shallow a transit it can detect.

        Astrophysical terms

        Exoplanet
        A planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. Every planet catalogued here is an exoplanet.
        Host star
        The star a given exoplanet orbits, and the star an observer actually points a telescope at, since the planet itself is not directly visible.
        V magnitude
        Apparent brightness as seen from Earth. Lower numbers are brighter; each step of 1 is about 2.5× dimmer.
        Spectral type
        A classification of a star by surface temperature and color, from hottest (O, B, A) through intermediate (F, G) to coolest (K, M).
        Parallax
        The tiny apparent shift in a star's position as Earth orbits the Sun, used to measure stellar distance directly and precisely.
        Solar mass / solar radius
        Units of mass and size defined relative to the Sun, used throughout astronomy to describe other stars in familiar terms.
        Orbital period
        The time a planet takes to complete one full orbit of its star, and the interval at which its transits repeat.
        Orbital eccentricity
        A measure of how stretched, rather than circular, a planet's orbit is. Most hot Jupiters here have nearly circular orbits; a few do not.
        Impact parameter
        How close to the center of the star's disk a planet's path crosses, as seen from Earth. A planet crossing dead center produces a longer, deeper transit than one skimming the star's edge.
        Limb darkening
        The real effect of a star appearing dimmer toward its edge than its center. It gently rounds the bottom of a real transit's light curve; the simulated charts on this page do not model it.
        Hot Jupiter / Ultra-hot Jupiter
        A gas giant orbiting very close to its star, with short periods and high temperatures. "Ultra-hot" hosts are typically hot A or F-type stars exceeding ~2200K on the dayside.
        Warm Saturn / warm Jupiter
        A giant planet on a longer, more distant orbit than a typical hot Jupiter, usually taking a week or more to complete one orbit, and correspondingly cooler.
        Am star
        Short for metallic-line A star: a chemically peculiar A-type star with an excess of certain heavy elements in its atmosphere.
        Delta Scuti variable
        A class of pulsating star that brightens and dims on a timescale of hours from internal oscillation, unrelated to any orbiting planet.
        TESS Object of Interest (TOI)
        A candidate planet identified by NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite that has not yet been fully confirmed through follow-up observation.

        Sky map and finding terms

        Altitude and azimuth
        Altitude is the angle above the horizon; azimuth is the compass direction, measured from north (0°) through east (90°), south (180°) and west (270°). The sky map and plans give both.
        J2000
        The standard reference frame for star coordinates, fixed to the Earth's orientation on 1 January 2000. The Seestar app expects custom objects in J2000.
        Precession
        The slow wobble of Earth's axis that shifts every star's coordinates by about 50″ per year. The sky map corrects for it automatically.
        Plate solving
        Working out exactly which part of the sky a photo shows by matching its star pattern to a catalog. It gives the sky coordinates of every pixel.
        Proper motion
        A star's real movement across the sky, caused by its motion through space relative to the Sun. Usually tiny; for nearby stars like HD 189733 it is measurable within a few decades.
        Field rotation
        On an alt-azimuth mount the star field slowly rotates in the frame during a long session. Stacking and photometry software correct for it, but it is why alignment matters.

Cloud forecast go/no-go from Open-Meteo. Finder charts with comparison star suggestions. Light curve checker. Shareable links to any transit.

Sky map for Campbell River with a transit timeline, integrated star finder with name and coordinate search, observing plans with calendar export and printing, the plate-solved #1 Star Candidate photo, a detection margin calculator, the HOPS workflow, red light mode, KELT-19 A coordinates, and a new layout. Times now follow B.C.'s permanent UTC−7, correcting November to March events by one hour from the printed booklet. Upcoming-event detection now handles transits after midnight correctly.
